messages.subject: Posterior for spatial averages
messages.subject_clean: Posterior for spatial averages
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am working with a GLMM with spatial effects

Y(s)|\mu(s) ~ Gamma(\mu(s) , \phi)
log(\mu(s)) = X(s)\beta + u(s)

where Y(s) is the response of interest at location s, X(s) are known covariates and u(s) is the latent spatial effect. Model fitting with INLA went smoothly as well as predictions at a set of locations s_1, ..., s_N.

But I am interested in the posterior of the average value of Y(s) within a given area, approximated by the finite sum over my prediction locations: (1/N) \sum Y(s_i).

It seems to me this unavoidably requires the joint posterior for Y(s_i), or u(s_i), for i = 1, .., N. The number of prediction locations is large, N ~ 10^7.

Is there a good way to do this?

Thanks,
Paul

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Posterior for spatial averages
messages.body_plain:
For those kinds of predictions, posterior sampling with inla.posterior.sample() is easiest; the samples are based on the joint posterior approximation, so you can compute any functional of the samples to get a sample from the posterior distribution of those functionals.
Finn

messages.subject: Bayesian age-period-cohort analysis with INLA
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian age-period-cohort analysis with INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hello,I'm doing a projection using bayesian age-period-cohort analysis with INLA.
Here's the code:
counts <- read.csv("/Users/ironjian/Downloads/ironjian\ 4/death_counts.csv", header = T)
 pop <- read.csv("/Users/ironjian/Downloads/ironjian\ 4/total_popu.csv", header = T)
 agegroup = c("35-39", "40-44", "45-49", "50-54", "55-59", "60-64", "65-69", "70-74","75-79", "80-84")
us.APC = APCList(counts, pop, gf=5, agelab=agegroup)
 col <- c("grey20", "grey35", "grey50", "grey65", "grey75", "grey85")
 ratesByAge(us.APC, scale=100000, age=seq(37,82,5), per=1990:2019, col=col)
us.res = BAPC(us.APC, predict=list(npredict=10, retro=TRUE))
sh: /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.1/Resources/library/INLA/bin/mac/64bit/inla: Permission denied
Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does help; please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.
What's the problem?
Thanks , sincerely looking forward to your reply.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] mgcv baseline equivalent
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] mgcv baseline equivalent
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jonathan,

I am considering similar problems to you, I am using rw2 models for smoothers on continuous covariates and I cannot figure out how to decide what priors to use for these effects, did you come up with an idea for yourself?

Best wishes,

Sylvan

On Thursday, October 15, 2020 at 4:27:55 PM UTC+1 bach...@gmail.com wrote:
> Finn:
>
> Thanks very much for this thorough answer. This answers a lot of important questions. Variance/precision priors are actually a more intuitive way to control the wiggliness of the function for me, so I will take that option any time.
>
> However, I struggle with choosing a sensible hyperprior for the precision on the rw2, even using scale.model=TRUE. I have read the papers discussing how one derives the pc.prior for the rw2 precision, but that still begs the question of what we would expect the variance to be in the first place. Certainly, one can fit the model in mgcv first (not a bad idea for quick and dirty exploratory work) and use gam.vcomp to get mgcv's interpretation of its spline structure in terms of a variance with intervals, but frankly that doesn't seem to work very well when I try to translate if over. Putting mgcv to one side (there is no need here to just replicate whatever it does), I've also tried to base the rw2 precision off the precision for the outcome variable , the precision that is fit by INLA when using the variable as an iid, and even the simple precision for the variable in the dataset to which I am applying the rw2 prior. They tend to give me fairly similar (bad) answers, with even the default prior being much better.
>
> I understand that at the end of the day there is no substitute for knowing your problem and knowing your subject matter, but I would like to think I know both of those pretty well: it's the translation into a rw1 or rw2 structure that I am not finding intuitive, at least not yet. Is there any rule of thumb you or others like to use to get a sense of where the rw2 precision is likely to end up, perhaps a ratio to something else given the number of unique values or the ratio of the variance in the proposed rw2 predictor versus that of the outcome? I can certainly start with the default log gamma, move it up and down, and keep track of the WAIC conditional on the results being sensible. Maybe there just isn't an intuitive rule of thumb that works for most problems. That's ok: some problems are just tricky. But if there are any guidelines that anyone has found are useful in making educated guesses about a good rw2 precision / variance, I'd appreciate hearing about them.
>
> Thanks again.
>
> On Tue, Oct 13, 2020 at 4:09 AM Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > The rw2 model does not require a regular-spaced grid, since it implements the irregular location RW2 model from
> >   https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1467-9469.2008.00610.x
> > so that's the basic equivalent to the mgcv models.
> > There isn't a 1-1 mapping between mgcv models and inla models; both contain models the other doesn't, but there are some ways of getting equivalent models, and more ways to get similar models.
> >
> > The TPS itself is a bit annoying, since while (in an additive Gaussian noise setting) the point minimiser of the penalty is the same as the point minimiser for the basic undampened (intrinsic stationary) 2D SPDE model, the induced Bayesian prior isn't the same.  However, you could use an inla.rgeneric construction to implement it (Note: David Miller and others have done something similar in the other direction so that you might be able to use a version of the 2D spde models with mgcv, as a smoothing penalty model).
> >
> > To get 2D kronecker models, the "group" feature gives you a kronecker between an arbitrary inla model and another model (restricted to a subset of the models, but includes the rw2 model).
> >
> > For 3D models, any available 2D model can be grouped with rw2.
> >
> > For a model on continuous space, with data at irregular locations, you can use an SPDE model, with a triangulation mesh (the triangle nodes don't need to be located at the data points; the mesh just needs to be built to give a sufficiently fine spatial resolution for the function being modelled).
> >
> > The interface doesn't have a direct kronecker model for 2D models, but you can build your own with the inla.generic technique that lets you define arbitrary models yourself.
> >
> > I'm working on expanding the interface for spatial models so that user-define models can have an easier time combining models, by defining collections of 1D and 2D domains into a single mapping object, but there are other items above it on the todo-list.
> >
> > But there is the inla.row.kron() function, that can be used to help:
> > If a basic model is u ~ N(0, Q^-1), and the observation level is linked to the latent vector u via a linear combination multiplication
> >   eta = A u
> > then a kronecker model v ~ N(0, (Q2 x Q1)^-1) has linear combinations of the form
> >   eta = (A2 rowx A1) v
> > where rowx is the rowwise kronecker product implemented by inla.row.kron().
> > Using this, you just need to figure out the 1D models first, and then use the above to combine them.
> >
> > Finally, for Bayesian models, there is no universal way around setting the priors to reasonable values. There are attempts to produce "default priors", but they all rely on assumptions that are essentially equivalent to choosing priors in a specific way that is not applicable to all response variable models.
> > For example, the prior variance for a spatial field has very different interpretations in an additive Gaussian georeferenced model compared with in a log-Gaussian Cox process model, even though on the latent Gaussian level they look the same.
> > For intrinsic stationary models in inla, such as rw2, the scale.model=TRUE option can help you, by standardising the scale of the variance, but beyond that the user must have enough understanding of their own application to be able to choose reasonable parameters.
> >
> > PS. My focus is now more on non-intrinsic models (i.e. with non-infinite range parameters like the rw2 and TPS), and non-separable models; except for space x time, separable kronecker models are mostly avoided in geostatistical problems.
> >
> > Finn
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Tue, 13 Oct 2020 at 04:17, Jonathan Judge <bach...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > The mgcv package makes it fairly easy to set up a thin plate regression spline, even in multiple dimensions for measurements on different scales (e.g., angles, speed, or time).
> > >
> > > Consider the models: y ~ s(x1, x2) or even y ~ s(x1, x2, x3), with the x variables being vectors of different kinds of numeric measurements . The default "tp" basis tends to work quite well, but tensor / Kronecker options and others are of course available also.
> > >
> > > Is there an INLA equivalent for a multi-dimensional smoother for data like this that tends to work well with some default settings? If a mesh is required, are there reasonably robust settings that can be specified relative to quantiles or some other aspect of the x vectors?  Most mesh examples I have seen involve spatial coordinates only and even if they apply to my situation I am struggling to see what good defaults would be.
> > >
> > > For what it is worth, the one-dimensional spde smoother function provided by the BRINLA bri.adapt.prior works incredibly well and keeps much of the machinery under the hood; perhaps there is a generalizable multi-dimensional version of it? I am also aware of the rw2 / rw2d option, but it seems that may require a regularly-spaced lattice and I'm not sure that is desirable for this application (perhaps it is: others will know more than me).
> > >
> > > I have also tried Simon's ginla function, which may also offer an avenue, but I am not quite sure if it is what I am looking for either.
> > >
> > > Would appreciate any suggestions.  Many thanks.
> > >
> > > Jonathan
> > >
> > >
> > > --

> >
> >
> > --

messages.body_plain:
using

f(time, model="rw2", scale.model=TRUE,
hyper = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(U,0.01)))

then chose U according to the expected max size of the effect, like, with

family="poisson",

you might use  U=0.5

see the PC-prior paper for the motivation.

messages.body_plain:
The "set it and forget it" aspect of mgcv is awfully nice.  I don't disagree with anything Havard has suggested here.

In terms of "quick and dirty" splines to get a sense of what the data might show, I tend to: (1) use a uniform prior, (2) always use "scale.model=TRUE" if the structure supports it, (3) if there are more than ~ 100 distinct points in the vector, just round to the minimum extent necessary so the number of distinct points gets below 100 (inla.group is a more intellectually rigorous option to achieve this, but INLA does not automatically find cutpoints the same way that mgcv seems to do). pc.priors are always a good choice; I am fortunate to usually have enough data that my priors are primarily about enhancing regularization performance rather than avoiding disasters, so the uniform is often a good place to start for me.  And a uniform prior is arguably what mgcv "assumes" anyway so it should generate somewhat similar results, a lot of the time.

It also may help to see these structures as a sequence of sorts.  If you have a continuous predictor that can be non-linear in places, start by modeling it as an iid; the iid structure has no idea of an overall trend and yet often does a surprisingly reasonable job in a transparent way.  See what the values look like.  Then try the same structure as an AR1 or RW1.  See what it looks like.  Then see what it looks like as RW2.  Track the WAIC values to see if you are more likely gaining information or noise.  Always use scale.model=TRUE when you can.  You'll get the feel for it.  Being focused on something only being an RW2 option could be leaving some accuracy on the table.

Jonathan

> > > > exploratory work) and use gam.vcomp to get mgcv's interpretation
> > > > of its spline structure in terms of a variance with intervals, but
> > > > frankly that doesn't seem to work very well when I try to
> > > > translate if over. Putting mgcv to one side (there is no need here
> > > > to just replicate whatever it does), I've also tried to base the
> > > > rw2 precision off the precision for the outcome variable , the
> > > > precision that is fit by INLA when using the variable as an iid,
> > > > and even the simple precision for the variable in the dataset to
> > > > which I am applying the rw2 prior. They tend to give me fairly
> > > > similar (bad) answers, with even the default prior being much
> > > > better.
> > > >
> > > > I understand that at the end of the day there is no substitute for
> > > > knowing your problem and knowing your subject matter, but I would
> > > > like to think I know both of those pretty well: it's the
> > > > translation into a rw1 or rw2 structure that I am not finding
> > > > intuitive, at least not yet. Is there any rule of thumb you or
> > > > others like to use to get a sense of where the rw2 precision is
> > > > likely to end up, perhaps a ratio to something else given the
> > > > number of unique values or the ratio of the variance in the
> > > > proposed rw2 predictor versus that of the outcome? I can certainly
> > > > start with the default log gamma, move it up and down, and keep
> > > > track of the WAIC conditional on the results being sensible. Maybe
> > > > there just isn't an intuitive rule of thumb that works for most
> > > > problems. That's ok: some problems are just tricky. But if there
> > > > are any guidelines that anyone has found are useful in making
> > > > educated guesses about a good rw2 precision / variance, I'd
> > > > appreciate hearing about them.
> > > >
> > > > Thanks again.
> > > >
> > > > On Tue, Oct 13, 2020 at 4:09 AM Finn Lindgren
> > > > <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Hi,
> > > > >
> > > > > The rw2 model does not require a regular-spaced grid, since it
> > > > > implements the irregular location RW2 model from
> > > > >
> > > > > https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1467-9469.2008.00610.x
> > > > > so that's the basic equivalent to the mgcv models.
> > > > > There isn't a 1-1 mapping between mgcv models and inla models;
> > > > > both contain models the other doesn't, but there are some ways
> > > > > of getting equivalent models, and more ways to get similar
> > > > > models.
> > > > >
> > > > > The TPS itself is a bit annoying, since while (in an additive
> > > > > Gaussian noise setting) the point minimiser of the penalty is
> > > > > the same as the point minimiser for the basic undampened
> > > > > (intrinsic stationary) 2D SPDE model, the induced Bayesian prior
> > > > > isn't the same.  However, you could use an
> > > > > inla.rgeneric construction to implement it (Note: David Miller
> > > > > and others have done something similar in the other direction so
> > > > > that you might be able to use a version of the 2D spde models
> > > > > with mgcv, as a smoothing penalty model).
> > > > >
> > > > > To get 2D kronecker models, the "group" feature gives you a
> > > > > kronecker between an arbitrary inla model and another model
> > > > > (restricted to a subset of the models, but includes the rw2
> > > > > model).
> > > > >
> > > > > For 3D models, any available 2D model can be grouped with rw2.
> > > > >
> > > > > For a model on continuous space, with data at irregular
> > > > > locations, you can use an SPDE model, with a triangulation mesh
> > > > > (the triangle nodes don't need to be located at the data points;
> > > > > the mesh just needs to be built to give a sufficiently fine
> > > > > spatial resolution for the function being modelled).
> > > > >
> > > > > The interface doesn't have a direct kronecker model for 2D
> > > > > models, but you can build your own with the
> > > > > inla.generic technique that lets you define arbitrary models
> > > > > yourself.
> > > > >
> > > > > I'm working on expanding the interface for spatial models so
> > > > > that user-define models can have an easier time combining
> > > > > models, by defining collections of 1D and 2D domains into a
> > > > > single mapping object, but there are other items above it on the
> > > > > todo-list.
> > > > >
> > > > > But there is the inla.row.kron() function, that can be used to
> > > > > help:
> > > > > If a basic model is u ~ N(0, Q^-1), and the observation level is
> > > > > linked to the latent vector u via a linear combination
> > > > > multiplication
> > > > >   eta = A u
> > > > > then a kronecker model v ~ N(0, (Q2 x Q1)^-1) has linear
> > > > > combinations of the form
> > > > >   eta = (A2 rowx A1) v
> > > > > where rowx is the rowwise kronecker product implemented by
> > > > > inla.row.kron().
> > > > > Using this, you just need to figure out the 1D models first, and
> > > > > then use the above to combine them.
> > > > >
> > > > > Finally, for Bayesian models, there is no universal way around
> > > > > setting the priors to reasonable values. There are attempts to
> > > > > produce "default priors", but they all rely on assumptions that
> > > > > are essentially equivalent to choosing priors in a specific way
> > > > > that is not applicable to all response variable models.
> > > > > For example, the prior variance for a spatial field has very
> > > > > different interpretations in an additive Gaussian georeferenced
> > > > > model compared with in a log-Gaussian Cox process model, even
> > > > > though on the latent Gaussian level they look the same.
> > > > > For intrinsic stationary models in inla, such as rw2, the
> > > > > scale.model=TRUE option can help you, by standardising the scale
> > > > > of the variance, but beyond that the user must have enough
> > > > > understanding of their own application to be able to choose
> > > > > reasonable parameters.
> > > > >
> > > > > PS. My focus is now more on non-intrinsic models (i.e. with non-
> > > > > infinite range parameters like the rw2 and TPS), and non-
> > > > > separable models; except for space x time, separable kronecker
> > > > > models are mostly avoided in geostatistical problems.
> > > > >
> > > > > Finn
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Tue, 13 Oct 2020 at 04:17, Jonathan Judge <bach...@gmail.com>
> > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > The mgcv package makes it fairly easy to set up a thin plate
> > > > > > regression spline, even in multiple dimensions for
> > > > > > measurements on different scales (e.g., angles, speed, or
> > > > > > time).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Consider the models: y ~ s(x1, x2) or even y ~ s(x1, x2, x3),
> > > > > > with the x variables being vectors of different kinds of
> > > > > > numeric measurements . The default "tp" basis tends to work
> > > > > > quite well, but tensor / Kronecker options and others are of
> > > > > > course available also.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Is there an INLA equivalent for a multi-dimensional smoother
> > > > > > for data like this that tends to work well with some default
> > > > > > settings? If a mesh is required, are there reasonably robust
> > > > > > settings that can be specified relative to quantiles or some
> > > > > > other aspect of the x vectors?  Most mesh examples I have seen
> > > > > > involve spatial coordinates only and even if they apply to my
> > > > > > situation I am struggling to see what good defaults would be.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > For what it is worth, the one-dimensional spde smoother
> > > > > > function provided by the BRINLA bri.adapt.prior works
> > > > > > incredibly well and keeps much of the machinery under the
> > > > > > hood; perhaps there is a generalizable multi-dimensional
> > > > > > version of it? I am also aware of the rw2 / rw2d option, but
> > > > > > it seems that may require a regularly-spaced lattice and I'm
> > > > > > not sure that is desirable for this application (perhaps it
> > > > > > is: others will know more than me).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I have also tried Simon's ginla function, which may also offer
> > > > > > an avenue, but I am not quite sure if it is what I am looking
> > > > > > for either.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Would appreciate any suggestions.  Many thanks.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Jonathan

messages.subject: Areal data and preferential sampling with inlabru
messages.subject_clean: Areal data and preferential sampling with inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA team,

I am working with a regular grid which aggregates counts of individuals in pixels with an area of approximately 10 km². Through the inlabru package, I defined the SPDE and I was able to fit a log Gaussian Poisson regression model to predict the overall abundance of my individuals in the whole study area.

However, my dataset might suffer of selection bias, due to the fact that I have sampled my data mostly were they were more available. This should be a case of preferential sampling.  As pointed out to me by Finn, with inlabru there is already a way to account for preferential sampling when dealing with an LGCP <https://github.com/inlabru-org/inlabru/issues/57>.

The problem is that my type of response is different, because I only consider counts. So far, I've just found this paper <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12803> where authors create a joint model through the use of INLA and TMB to account for preferential sampling in areal data.

Since the procedure illustrated in inlabru for LGCP model looked more straightforward, I was wondering if something similar has already been implemented in a more "user-friendly" inlabru way.

Thank you as always for your help and best regards.

Nico

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

I am basically working under the assumption that my counts come from a preferential sampling which might be dependent on the underlying GRF. If you check the attached image of Switzerland, it shows more abundance in the city areas because in such areas there were more information where to collect counts from. If I have understood correctly, this might lead to underestimation of what's happening in the rural areas. For this reason, I was thinking to apply the LGCP example, but to my counts.

According to your answer, I can always define my SPDE in the usual way, but the likelihoods should change in the following way?

lik1 <- like(data = grid, # SpatialPixelsDataFrame
                  family = "poisson",
                  formula = abundance ~ covariate(s) + # I have them at the pixel level
                                    spde +
                                    Intercept)

lik2 <- like(data = grid,
                   family = "poisson",
                   domain = list(coordinates = mesh),
                   formula = coordinates ~ spdeCopy + countIntercept)

Thanks again for your answer!

Nico

messages.subject: Beginner Question: Prior Specification (Logistic Regression)
messages.subject_clean: Beginner Question: Prior Specification (Logistic Regression)
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I am trying to fit a Logistic regression model using R-INLA. I have 3 covariates and I am interested in using a non-informative prior for two of them, but an informative prior for the other. It seems like I could write the code as follows for a non-informative/default prior for all parameters:

model1<-inla(RESPONSE ~ TRT+ AGE + LUNG_Capacity + WB_Count,
           data=dataset1, family = "binomial", Ntrials = 1, num.threads = 2)

However, if I want to use an informative prior for LUNG_Capacity (from among the available standard options - Gaussian should do, I don't need a custom prior), its not intuitive to me what the syntax is. All examples online seem to be for the case where you only have a single variable for which you are specifying a prior.

Thanks for any help. Long time JAGS user, trying to make the leap to INLA! If this has already been answered, I'd be grateful for a link (although a search on this forum didnt seem to help).

Regards
Desi.

messages.body_plain:
Since the basic covariate effects are Gaussian, the easiest way to change the precision parameter is to replace + LUNG_capacity with
  + f(LUNG_capacity, model="linear", prec.linear = ...)
where ... is the desired precicion for the prior for the LUNG_capacity parameter. You can also change the mean with mean.linear.
See ?INLA::f and search for prec.linear, which also reveals you can get the default value via
  INLA::inla.set.control.fixed.default()$prec

Finn

> In terms of "quick and dirty" splines to get a sense of what the data might show, I tend to: (1) use a uniform prior, (2) always use "scale.model=TRUE" if the structure supports it, (3) if there are more than ~ 100 distinct points in the vector, just round to the minimum extent necessary so the number of distinct points gets below 100 (inla.group is a more intellectually rigorous option to achieve this, but INLA does not automatically find cutpoints the same way that mgcv seems to do). pc.priors are always a good choice; I am fortunate to usually have enough data that my priors are primarily about enhancing regularization performance rather than avoiding disasters, so the uniform is often a good place to start for me.  And a uniform prior is arguably what mgcv "assumes" anyway so it should generate somewhat similar results, a lot of the time.
>
> It also may help to see these structures as a sequence of sorts.  If you have a continuous predictor that can be non-linear in places, start by modeling it as an iid; the iid structure has no idea of an overall trend and yet often does a surprisingly reasonable job in a transparent way.  See what the values look like.  Then try the same structure as an AR1 or RW1.  See what it looks like.  Then see what it looks like as RW2.  Track the WAIC values to see if you are more likely gaining information or noise.  Always use scale.model=TRUE when you can.  You'll get the feel for it.  Being focused on something only being an RW2 option could be leaving some accuracy on the table.
>

> > > > > Finn:
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks very much for this thorough answer. This answers a lot of
> > > > > important questions. Variance/precision priors are actually a more
> > > > > intuitive way to control the wiggliness of the function for me, so
> > > > > I will take that option any time.
> > > > >
> > > > > However, I struggle with choosing a sensible hyperprior for the
> > > > > precision on the rw2, even using scale.model=TRUE. I have read the
> > > > > papers discussing how one derives the pc.prior for the rw2
> > > > > precision, but that still begs the question of what we would
> > > > > expect the variance to be in the first place. Certainly, one can
> > > > > fit the model in mgcv first (not a bad idea for quick and dirty
> > > > > exploratory work) and use gam.vcomp to get mgcv's interpretation
> > > > > of its spline structure in terms of a variance with intervals, but
> > > > > frankly that doesn't seem to work very well when I try to
> > > > > translate if over. Putting mgcv to one side (there is no need here
> > > > > to just replicate whatever it does), I've also tried to base the
> > > > > rw2 precision off the precision for the outcome variable , the
> > > > > precision that is fit by INLA when using the variable as an iid,
> > > > > and even the simple precision for the variable in the dataset to
> > > > > which I am applying the rw2 prior. They tend to give me fairly
> > > > > similar (bad) answers, with even the default prior being much
> > > > > better.

> > > > > knowing your problem and knowing your subject matter, but I would
> > > > > like to think I know both of those pretty well: it's the
> > > > > translation into a rw1 or rw2 structure that I am not finding
> > > > > intuitive, at least not yet. Is there any rule of thumb you or
> > > > > others like to use to get a sense of where the rw2 precision is
> > > > > likely to end up, perhaps a ratio to something else given the
> > > > > number of unique values or the ratio of the variance in the
> > > > > proposed rw2 predictor versus that of the outcome? I can certainly
> > > > > start with the default log gamma, move it up and down, and keep
> > > > > track of the WAIC conditional on the results being sensible. Maybe
> > > > > there just isn't an intuitive rule of thumb that works for most
> > > > > problems. That's ok: some problems are just tricky. But if there
> > > > > are any guidelines that anyone has found are useful in making
> > > > > educated guesses about a good rw2 precision / variance, I'd
> > > > > appreciate hearing about them.
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks again.
> > > > >
> > > > > On Tue, Oct 13, 2020 at 4:09 AM Finn Lindgren
> > > > > <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The rw2 model does not require a regular-spaced grid, since it
> > > > > > implements the irregular location RW2 model from
> > > > > >
> > > > > > https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1467-9469.2008.00610.x
> > > > > > so that's the basic equivalent to the mgcv models.
> > > > > > There isn't a 1-1 mapping between mgcv models and inla models;
> > > > > > both contain models the other doesn't, but there are some ways
> > > > > > of getting equivalent models, and more ways to get similar
> > > > > > models.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The TPS itself is a bit annoying, since while (in an additive
> > > > > > Gaussian noise setting) the point minimiser of the penalty is
> > > > > > the same as the point minimiser for the basic undampened
> > > > > > (intrinsic stationary) 2D SPDE model, the induced Bayesian prior
> > > > > > isn't the same.  However, you could use an
> > > > > > inla.rgeneric construction to implement it (Note: David Miller
> > > > > > and others have done something similar in the other direction so
> > > > > > that you might be able to use a version of the 2D spde models
> > > > > > with mgcv, as a smoothing penalty model).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > To get 2D kronecker models, the "group" feature gives you a
> > > > > > kronecker between an arbitrary inla model and another model
> > > > > > (restricted to a subset of the models, but includes the rw2
> > > > > > model).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > For 3D models, any available 2D model can be grouped with rw2.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > For a model on continuous space, with data at irregular
> > > > > > locations, you can use an SPDE model, with a triangulation mesh
> > > > > > (the triangle nodes don't need to be located at the data points;
> > > > > > the mesh just needs to be built to give a sufficiently fine
> > > > > > spatial resolution for the function being modelled).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The interface doesn't have a direct kronecker model for 2D
> > > > > > models, but you can build your own with the
> > > > > > inla.generic technique that lets you define arbitrary models
> > > > > > yourself.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I'm working on expanding the interface for spatial models so
> > > > > > that user-define models can have an easier time combining
> > > > > > models, by defining collections of 1D and 2D domains into a
> > > > > > single mapping object, but there are other items above it on the
> > > > > > todo-list.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > But there is the inla.row.kron() function, that can be used to
> > > > > > help:
> > > > > > If a basic model is u ~ N(0, Q^-1), and the observation level is
> > > > > > linked to the latent vector u via a linear combination
> > > > > > multiplication
> > > > > >   eta = A u
> > > > > > then a kronecker model v ~ N(0, (Q2 x Q1)^-1) has linear
> > > > > > combinations of the form
> > > > > >   eta = (A2 rowx A1) v
> > > > > > where rowx is the rowwise kronecker product implemented by
> > > > > > inla.row.kron().
> > > > > > Using this, you just need to figure out the 1D models first, and
> > > > > > then use the above to combine them.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Finally, for Bayesian models, there is no universal way around
> > > > > > setting the priors to reasonable values. There are attempts to
> > > > > > produce "default priors", but they all rely on assumptions that
> > > > > > are essentially equivalent to choosing priors in a specific way
> > > > > > that is not applicable to all response variable models.
> > > > > > For example, the prior variance for a spatial field has very
> > > > > > different interpretations in an additive Gaussian georeferenced
> > > > > > model compared with in a log-Gaussian Cox process model, even
> > > > > > though on the latent Gaussian level they look the same.
> > > > > > For intrinsic stationary models in inla, such as rw2, the
> > > > > > scale.model=TRUE option can help you, by standardising the scale
> > > > > > of the variance, but beyond that the user must have enough
> > > > > > understanding of their own application to be able to choose
> > > > > > reasonable parameters.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > PS. My focus is now more on non-intrinsic models (i.e. with non-
> > > > > > infinite range parameters like the rw2 and TPS), and non-
> > > > > > separable models; except for space x time, separable kronecker
> > > > > > models are mostly avoided in geostatistical problems.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Finn
> > > > > >
> > > > > >

> > > > > > > measurements on different scales (e.g., angles, speed, or
> > > > > > > time).

> > > > > > > Consider the models: y ~ s(x1, x2) or even y ~ s(x1, x2, x3),
> > > > > > > with the x variables being vectors of different kinds of
> > > > > > > numeric measurements . The default "tp" basis tends to work
> > > > > > > quite well, but tensor / Kronecker options and others are of
> > > > > > > course available also.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Is there an INLA equivalent for a multi-dimensional smoother
> > > > > > > for data like this that tends to work well with some default
> > > > > > > settings? If a mesh is required, are there reasonably robust
> > > > > > > settings that can be specified relative to quantiles or some
> > > > > > > other aspect of the x vectors?  Most mesh examples I have seen
> > > > > > > involve spatial coordinates only and even if they apply to my
> > > > > > > situation I am struggling to see what good defaults would be.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > For what it is worth, the one-dimensional spde smoother
> > > > > > > function provided by the BRINLA bri.adapt.prior works
> > > > > > > incredibly well and keeps much of the machinery under the
> > > > > > > hood; perhaps there is a generalizable multi-dimensional
> > > > > > > version of it? I am also aware of the rw2 / rw2d option, but
> > > > > > > it seems that may require a regularly-spaced lattice and I'm
> > > > > > > not sure that is desirable for this application (perhaps it
> > > > > > > is: others will know more than me).
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I have also tried Simon's ginla function, which may also offer
> > > > > > > an avenue, but I am not quite sure if it is what I am looking
> > > > > > > for either.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Would appreciate any suggestions.  Many thanks.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Jonathan

> > > > > > > But there is the inla.row.kron() function, that can be
> > > > > > > used to
> > > > > > > help:
> > > > > > > If a basic model is u ~ N(0, Q^-1), and the observation
> > > > > > > level is
> > > > > > > linked to the latent vector u via a linear combination
> > > > > > > multiplication
> > > > > > >   eta = A u
> > > > > > > then a kronecker model v ~ N(0, (Q2 x Q1)^-1) has linear
> > > > > > > combinations of the form
> > > > > > >   eta = (A2 rowx A1) v
> > > > > > > where rowx is the rowwise kronecker product implemented by
> > > > > > > inla.row.kron().
> > > > > > > Using this, you just need to figure out the 1D models
> > > > > > > first, and
> > > > > > > then use the above to combine them.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Finally, for Bayesian models, there is no universal way
> > > > > > > around
> > > > > > > setting the priors to reasonable values. There are
> > > > > > > attempts to
> > > > > > > produce "default priors", but they all rely on assumptions
> > > > > > > that
> > > > > > > are essentially equivalent to choosing priors in a
> > > > > > > specific way
> > > > > > > that is not applicable to all response variable models.
> > > > > > > For example, the prior variance for a spatial field has
> > > > > > > very
> > > > > > > different interpretations in an additive Gaussian
> > > > > > > georeferenced
> > > > > > > model compared with in a log-Gaussian Cox process model,
> > > > > > > even
> > > > > > > though on the latent Gaussian level they look the same.
> > > > > > > For intrinsic stationary models in inla, such as rw2, the
> > > > > > > scale.model=TRUE option can help you, by standardising the
> > > > > > > scale
> > > > > > > of the variance, but beyond that the user must have enough
> > > > > > > understanding of their own application to be able to
> > > > > > > choose
> > > > > > > reasonable parameters.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > PS. My focus is now more on non-intrinsic models (i.e.
> > > > > > > with non-
> > > > > > > infinite range parameters like the rw2 and TPS), and non-
> > > > > > > separable models; except for space x time, separable
> > > > > > > kronecker
> > > > > > > models are mostly avoided in geostatistical problems.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Finn
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Tue, 13 Oct 2020 at 04:17, Jonathan Judge
> > > > > > > <bach...@gmail.com>
> > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > > The mgcv package makes it fairly easy to set up a thin
> > > > > > > > plate
> > > > > > > > regression spline, even in multiple dimensions for
> > > > > > > > measurements on different scales (e.g., angles, speed,
> > > > > > > > or
> > > > > > > > time).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Consider the models: y ~ s(x1, x2) or even y ~ s(x1, x2,
> > > > > > > > x3),
> > > > > > > > with the x variables being vectors of different kinds of
> > > > > > > > numeric measurements . The default "tp" basis tends to
> > > > > > > > work
> > > > > > > > quite well, but tensor / Kronecker options and others
> > > > > > > > are of
> > > > > > > > course available also.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Is there an INLA equivalent for a multi-dimensional
> > > > > > > > smoother
> > > > > > > > for data like this that tends to work well with some
> > > > > > > > default
> > > > > > > > settings? If a mesh is required, are there reasonably
> > > > > > > > robust
> > > > > > > > settings that can be specified relative to quantiles or
> > > > > > > > some
> > > > > > > > other aspect of the x vectors?  Most mesh examples I
> > > > > > > > have seen
> > > > > > > > involve spatial coordinates only and even if they apply
> > > > > > > > to my
> > > > > > > > situation I am struggling to see what good defaults
> > > > > > > > would be.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > For what it is worth, the one-dimensional spde smoother
> > > > > > > > function provided by the BRINLA bri.adapt.prior works
> > > > > > > > incredibly well and keeps much of the machinery under
> > > > > > > > the
> > > > > > > > hood; perhaps there is a generalizable multi-dimensional
> > > > > > > > version of it? I am also aware of the rw2 / rw2d option,
> > > > > > > > but
> > > > > > > > it seems that may require a regularly-spaced lattice and
> > > > > > > > I'm
> > > > > > > > not sure that is desirable for this application (perhaps
> > > > > > > > it
> > > > > > > > is: others will know more than me).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I have also tried Simon's ginla function, which may also
> > > > > > > > offer
> > > > > > > > an avenue, but I am not quite sure if it is what I am
> > > > > > > > looking
> > > > > > > > for either.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Would appreciate any suggestions.  Many thanks.

> > > The "set it and forget it" aspect of mgcv is awfully nice.  I don't
> > > disagree with anything Havard has suggested here.
> > >
> > > In terms of "quick and dirty" splines to get a sense of what the
> > > data might show, I tend to: (1) use a uniform prior, (2) always use
> > > "scale.model=TRUE" if the structure supports it, (3) if there are
> > > more than ~ 100 distinct points in the vector, just round to the
> > > minimum extent necessary so the number of distinct points gets below
> > > 100 (inla.group is a more intellectually rigorous option to achieve
> > > this, but INLA does not automatically find cutpoints the same way
> > > that mgcv seems to do). pc.priors are always a good choice; I am
> > > fortunate to usually have enough data that my priors are primarily
> > > about enhancing regularization performance rather than avoiding
> > > disasters, so the uniform is often a good place to start for me.
> > > And a uniform prior is arguably what mgcv "assumes" anyway so it
> > > should generate somewhat similar results, a lot of the time.
> > >
> > > It also may help to see these structures as a sequence of sorts.  If
> > > you have a continuous predictor that can be non-linear in places,
> > > start by modeling it as an iid; the iid structure has no idea of an
> > > overall trend and yet often does a surprisingly reasonable job in a
> > > transparent way.  See what the values look like.  Then try the same
> > > structure as an AR1 or RW1.  See what it looks like.  Then see what
> > > it looks like as RW2.  Track the WAIC values to see if you are more
> > > likely gaining information or noise.  Always use scale.model=TRUE
> > > when you can.  You'll get the feel for it.  Being focused on
> > > something only being an RW2 option could be leaving some accuracy on
> > > the table.
> > >
> > > Jonathan

> > > > > > > On Tue, Oct 13, 2020 at 4:09 AM Finn Lindgren
> > > > > > > <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > The rw2 model does not require a regular-spaced grid,
> > > > > > > > since it
> > > > > > > > implements the irregular location RW2 model from
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1467-9469.2008.00610.x
> > > > > > > > so that's the basic equivalent to the mgcv models.
> > > > > > > > There isn't a 1-1 mapping between mgcv models and inla
> > > > > > > > models;
> > > > > > > > both contain models the other doesn't, but there are some
> > > > > > > > ways
> > > > > > > > of getting equivalent models, and more ways to get similar
> > > > > > > > models.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > The TPS itself is a bit annoying, since while (in an
> > > > > > > > additive
> > > > > > > > Gaussian noise setting) the point minimiser of the
> > > > > > > > penalty is
> > > > > > > > the same as the point minimiser for the basic undampened
> > > > > > > > (intrinsic stationary) 2D SPDE model, the induced Bayesian
> > > > > > > > prior
> > > > > > > > isn't the same.  However, you could use an
> > > > > > > > inla.rgeneric construction to implement it (Note: David
> > > > > > > > Miller
> > > > > > > > and others have done something similar in the other
> > > > > > > > direction so
> > > > > > > > that you might be able to use a version of the 2D spde
> > > > > > > > models
> > > > > > > > with mgcv, as a smoothing penalty model).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > To get 2D kronecker models, the "group" feature gives you
> > > > > > > > a
> > > > > > > > kronecker between an arbitrary inla model and another
> > > > > > > > model
> > > > > > > > (restricted to a subset of the models, but includes the
> > > > > > > > rw2
> > > > > > > > model).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > For 3D models, any available 2D model can be grouped with
> > > > > > > > rw2.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > For a model on continuous space, with data at irregular
> > > > > > > > locations, you can use an SPDE model, with a triangulation
> > > > > > > > mesh
> > > > > > > > (the triangle nodes don't need to be located at the data
> > > > > > > > points;
> > > > > > > > the mesh just needs to be built to give a sufficiently
> > > > > > > > fine
> > > > > > > > spatial resolution for the function being modelled).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > The interface doesn't have a direct kronecker model for 2D
> > > > > > > > models, but you can build your own with the
> > > > > > > > inla.generic technique that lets you define arbitrary
> > > > > > > > models
> > > > > > > > yourself.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I'm working on expanding the interface for spatial models
> > > > > > > > so
> > > > > > > > that user-define models can have an easier time combining
> > > > > > > > models, by defining collections of 1D and 2D domains into
> > > > > > > > a
> > > > > > > > single mapping object, but there are other items above it
> > > > > > > > on the
> > > > > > > > todo-list.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > But there is the inla.row.kron() function, that can be
> > > > > > > > used to
> > > > > > > > help:
> > > > > > > > If a basic model is u ~ N(0, Q^-1), and the observation
> > > > > > > > level is
> > > > > > > > linked to the latent vector u via a linear combination
> > > > > > > > multiplication
> > > > > > > >   eta = A u
> > > > > > > > then a kronecker model v ~ N(0, (Q2 x Q1)^-1) has linear
> > > > > > > > combinations of the form
> > > > > > > >   eta = (A2 rowx A1) v
> > > > > > > > where rowx is the rowwise kronecker product implemented by
> > > > > > > > inla.row.kron().
> > > > > > > > Using this, you just need to figure out the 1D models
> > > > > > > > first, and
> > > > > > > > then use the above to combine them.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Finally, for Bayesian models, there is no universal way
> > > > > > > > around
> > > > > > > > setting the priors to reasonable values. There are
> > > > > > > > attempts to
> > > > > > > > produce "default priors", but they all rely on assumptions
> > > > > > > > that
> > > > > > > > are essentially equivalent to choosing priors in a
> > > > > > > > specific way
> > > > > > > > that is not applicable to all response variable models.
> > > > > > > > For example, the prior variance for a spatial field has
> > > > > > > > very
> > > > > > > > different interpretations in an additive Gaussian
> > > > > > > > georeferenced
> > > > > > > > model compared with in a log-Gaussian Cox process model,
> > > > > > > > even
> > > > > > > > though on the latent Gaussian level they look the same.
> > > > > > > > For intrinsic stationary models in inla, such as rw2, the
> > > > > > > > scale.model=TRUE option can help you, by standardising the
> > > > > > > > scale
> > > > > > > > of the variance, but beyond that the user must have enough
> > > > > > > > understanding of their own application to be able to
> > > > > > > > choose
> > > > > > > > reasonable parameters.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > PS. My focus is now more on non-intrinsic models (i.e.
> > > > > > > > with non-
> > > > > > > > infinite range parameters like the rw2 and TPS), and non-
> > > > > > > > separable models; except for space x time, separable
> > > > > > > > kronecker
> > > > > > > > models are mostly avoided in geostatistical problems.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Finn
> > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > On Tue, 13 Oct 2020 at 04:17, Jonathan Judge
> > > > > > > > <bach...@gmail.com>
> > > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > > > The mgcv package makes it fairly easy to set up a thin
> > > > > > > > > plate
> > > > > > > > > regression spline, even in multiple dimensions for
> > > > > > > > > measurements on different scales (e.g., angles, speed,

> > > > > > > > > time).
> > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > numeric measurements . The default "tp" basis tends to
> > > > > > > > > work

> > > > > > > > > Is there an INLA equivalent for a multi-dimensional
> > > > > > > > > smoother
> > > > > > > > > for data like this that tends to work well with some
> > > > > > > > > default
> > > > > > > > > settings? If a mesh is required, are there reasonably

> > > > > > > > > settings that can be specified relative to quantiles or

> > > > > > > > > other aspect of the x vectors?  Most mesh examples I
> > > > > > > > > have seen
> > > > > > > > > involve spatial coordinates only and even if they apply
> > > > > > > > > to my
> > > > > > > > > situation I am struggling to see what good defaults

> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > For what it is worth, the one-dimensional spde smoother
> > > > > > > > > function provided by the BRINLA bri.adapt.prior works

> > > > > > > > > hood; perhaps there is a generalizable multi-dimensional

> > > > > > > > > but
> > > > > > > > > it seems that may require a regularly-spaced lattice and
> > > > > > > > > I'm
> > > > > > > > > not sure that is desirable for this application (perhaps
> > > > > > > > > it
> > > > > > > > > is: others will know more than me).
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I have also tried Simon's ginla function, which may also

> > > > > > > > > an avenue, but I am not quite sure if it is what I am

> > > > > > > > > for either.

> > > > > > > > > Would appreciate any suggestions.  Many thanks.

> > > > The "set it and forget it" aspect of mgcv is awfully nice.  I
> > > > don't
> > > > disagree with anything Havard has suggested here.
> > > >
> > > > In terms of "quick and dirty" splines to get a sense of what the
> > > > data might show, I tend to: (1) use a uniform prior, (2) always
> > > > use
> > > > "scale.model=TRUE" if the structure supports it, (3) if there
> > > > are
> > > > more than ~ 100 distinct points in the vector, just round to the
> > > > minimum extent necessary so the number of distinct points gets
> > > > below
> > > > 100 (inla.group is a more intellectually rigorous option to
> > > > achieve
> > > > this, but INLA does not automatically find cutpoints the same
> > > > way
> > > > that mgcv seems to do). pc.priors are always a good choice; I am
> > > > fortunate to usually have enough data that my priors are
> > > > primarily
> > > > about enhancing regularization performance rather than avoiding
> > > > disasters, so the uniform is often a good place to start for
> > > > me.
> > > > And a uniform prior is arguably what mgcv "assumes" anyway so it
> > > > should generate somewhat similar results, a lot of the time.
> > > >
> > > > It also may help to see these structures as a sequence of
> > > > sorts.  If
> > > > you have a continuous predictor that can be non-linear in
> > > > places,
> > > > start by modeling it as an iid; the iid structure has no idea of
> > > > an
> > > > overall trend and yet often does a surprisingly reasonable job
> > > > in a
> > > > transparent way.  See what the values look like.  Then try the
> > > > same
> > > > structure as an AR1 or RW1.  See what it looks like.  Then see
> > > > what
> > > > it looks like as RW2.  Track the WAIC values to see if you are
> > > > more
> > > > likely gaining information or noise.  Always use
> > > > scale.model=TRUE
> > > > when you can.  You'll get the feel for it.  Being focused on
> > > > something only being an RW2 option could be leaving some
> > > > accuracy on
> > > > the table.
> > > >

> > > > > > > > for
> > > > > > > > me, so
> > > > > > > > I will take that option any time.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > However, I struggle with choosing a sensible hyperprior
> > > > > > > > for
> > > > > > > > the
> > > > > > > > precision on the rw2, even using scale.model=TRUE. I
> > > > > > > > have
> > > > > > > > read the
> > > > > > > > papers discussing how one derives the pc.prior for the
> > > > > > > > rw2
> > > > > > > > precision, but that still begs the question of what we
> > > > > > > > would
> > > > > > > > expect the variance to be in the first place. Certainly,
> > > > > > > > one
> > > > > > > > can
> > > > > > > > fit the model in mgcv first (not a bad idea for quick
> > > > > > > > and
> > > > > > > > dirty
> > > > > > > > exploratory work) and use gam.vcomp to get mgcv's
> > > > > > > > interpretation
> > > > > > > > of its spline structure in terms of a variance with
> > > > > > > > intervals, but
> > > > > > > > frankly that doesn't seem to work very well when I try
> > > > > > > > to
> > > > > > > > translate if over. Putting mgcv to one side (there is no
> > > > > > > > need here
> > > > > > > > to just replicate whatever it does), I've also tried to
> > > > > > > > base
> > > > > > > > the
> > > > > > > > rw2 precision off the precision for the outcome variable
> > > > > > > > ,
> > > > > > > > the
> > > > > > > > precision that is fit by INLA when using the variable as
> > > > > > > > an
> > > > > > > > iid,
> > > > > > > > and even the simple precision for the variable in the
> > > > > > > > dataset to
> > > > > > > > which I am applying the rw2 prior. They tend to give me
> > > > > > > > fairly
> > > > > > > > similar (bad) answers, with even the default prior being
> > > > > > > > much
> > > > > > > > better.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I understand that at the end of the day there is no
> > > > > > > > substitute for
> > > > > > > > knowing your problem and knowing your subject matter,
> > > > > > > > but I
> > > > > > > > would
> > > > > > > > like to think I know both of those pretty well: it's the
> > > > > > > > translation into a rw1 or rw2 structure that I am not
> > > > > > > > finding
> > > > > > > > intuitive, at least not yet. Is there any rule of thumb
> > > > > > > > you
> > > > > > > > or
> > > > > > > > others like to use to get a sense of where the rw2
> > > > > > > > precision
> > > > > > > > is
> > > > > > > > likely to end up, perhaps a ratio to something else
> > > > > > > > given
> > > > > > > > the
> > > > > > > > number of unique values or the ratio of the variance in
> > > > > > > > the
> > > > > > > > proposed rw2 predictor versus that of the outcome? I can
> > > > > > > > certainly
> > > > > > > > start with the default log gamma, move it up and down,
> > > > > > > > and
> > > > > > > > keep
> > > > > > > > track of the WAIC conditional on the results being
> > > > > > > > sensible.
> > > > > > > > Maybe
> > > > > > > > there just isn't an intuitive rule of thumb that works
> > > > > > > > for
> > > > > > > > most
> > > > > > > > problems. That's ok: some problems are just tricky. But
> > > > > > > > if
> > > > > > > > there
> > > > > > > > are any guidelines that anyone has found are useful in
> > > > > > > > making
> > > > > > > > educated guesses about a good rw2 precision / variance,
> > > > > > > > I'd

> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Thanks again.

> > > > > > > > On Tue, Oct 13, 2020 at 4:09 AM Finn Lindgren
> > > > > > > > <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > The rw2 model does not require a regular-spaced grid,
> > > > > > > > > since it
> > > > > > > > > implements the irregular location RW2 model from
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1467-9469.2008.00610.x
> > > > > > > > > so that's the basic equivalent to the mgcv models.
> > > > > > > > > There isn't a 1-1 mapping between mgcv models and inla
> > > > > > > > > models;
> > > > > > > > > both contain models the other doesn't, but there are
> > > > > > > > > some
> > > > > > > > > ways
> > > > > > > > > of getting equivalent models, and more ways to get
> > > > > > > > > similar
> > > > > > > > > models.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > The TPS itself is a bit annoying, since while (in an
> > > > > > > > > additive
> > > > > > > > > Gaussian noise setting) the point minimiser of the
> > > > > > > > > penalty is
> > > > > > > > > the same as the point minimiser for the basic
> > > > > > > > > undampened
> > > > > > > > > (intrinsic stationary) 2D SPDE model, the induced
> > > > > > > > > Bayesian
> > > > > > > > > prior
> > > > > > > > > isn't the same.  However, you could use an
> > > > > > > > > inla.rgeneric construction to implement it (Note:
> > > > > > > > > David
> > > > > > > > > Miller
> > > > > > > > > and others have done something similar in the other
> > > > > > > > > direction so
> > > > > > > > > that you might be able to use a version of the 2D spde
> > > > > > > > > models
> > > > > > > > > with mgcv, as a smoothing penalty model).
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > To get 2D kronecker models, the "group" feature gives
> > > > > > > > > you
> > > > > > > > > a
> > > > > > > > > kronecker between an arbitrary inla model and another
> > > > > > > > > model
> > > > > > > > > (restricted to a subset of the models, but includes
> > > > > > > > > the
> > > > > > > > > rw2
> > > > > > > > > model).
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > For 3D models, any available 2D model can be grouped
> > > > > > > > > with
> > > > > > > > > rw2.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > For a model on continuous space, with data at
> > > > > > > > > irregular
> > > > > > > > > locations, you can use an SPDE model, with a
> > > > > > > > > triangulation
> > > > > > > > > mesh
> > > > > > > > > (the triangle nodes don't need to be located at the
> > > > > > > > > data
> > > > > > > > > points;
> > > > > > > > > the mesh just needs to be built to give a sufficiently
> > > > > > > > > fine
> > > > > > > > > spatial resolution for the function being modelled).
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > The interface doesn't have a direct kronecker model
> > > > > > > > > for 2D
> > > > > > > > > models, but you can build your own with the
> > > > > > > > > inla.generic technique that lets you define arbitrary
> > > > > > > > > models
> > > > > > > > > yourself.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I'm working on expanding the interface for spatial
> > > > > > > > > models
> > > > > > > > > so
> > > > > > > > > that user-define models can have an easier time
> > > > > > > > > combining
> > > > > > > > > models, by defining collections of 1D and 2D domains
> > > > > > > > > into
> > > > > > > > > a
> > > > > > > > > single mapping object, but there are other items above
> > > > > > > > > it
> > > > > > > > > on the
> > > > > > > > > todo-list.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > But there is the inla.row.kron() function, that can be
> > > > > > > > > used to
> > > > > > > > > help:
> > > > > > > > > If a basic model is u ~ N(0, Q^-1), and the
> > > > > > > > > observation
> > > > > > > > > level is
> > > > > > > > > linked to the latent vector u via a linear combination
> > > > > > > > > multiplication
> > > > > > > > >   eta = A u
> > > > > > > > > then a kronecker model v ~ N(0, (Q2 x Q1)^-1) has
> > > > > > > > > linear
> > > > > > > > > combinations of the form
> > > > > > > > >   eta = (A2 rowx A1) v
> > > > > > > > > where rowx is the rowwise kronecker product
> > > > > > > > > implemented by
> > > > > > > > > inla.row.kron().
> > > > > > > > > Using this, you just need to figure out the 1D models
> > > > > > > > > first, and
> > > > > > > > > then use the above to combine them.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Finally, for Bayesian models, there is no universal
> > > > > > > > > way
> > > > > > > > > around
> > > > > > > > > setting the priors to reasonable values. There are
> > > > > > > > > attempts to
> > > > > > > > > produce "default priors", but they all rely on
> > > > > > > > > assumptions
> > > > > > > > > that
> > > > > > > > > are essentially equivalent to choosing priors in a
> > > > > > > > > specific way
> > > > > > > > > that is not applicable to all response variable
> > > > > > > > > models.
> > > > > > > > > For example, the prior variance for a spatial field
> > > > > > > > > has
> > > > > > > > > very
> > > > > > > > > different interpretations in an additive Gaussian
> > > > > > > > > georeferenced
> > > > > > > > > model compared with in a log-Gaussian Cox process
> > > > > > > > > model,
> > > > > > > > > even
> > > > > > > > > though on the latent Gaussian level they look the
> > > > > > > > > same.
> > > > > > > > > For intrinsic stationary models in inla, such as rw2,
> > > > > > > > > the
> > > > > > > > > scale.model=TRUE option can help you, by standardising
> > > > > > > > > the
> > > > > > > > > scale
> > > > > > > > > of the variance, but beyond that the user must have
> > > > > > > > > enough
> > > > > > > > > understanding of their own application to be able to
> > > > > > > > > choose
> > > > > > > > > reasonable parameters.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > PS. My focus is now more on non-intrinsic models (i.e.
> > > > > > > > > with non-
> > > > > > > > > infinite range parameters like the rw2 and TPS), and
> > > > > > > > > non-
> > > > > > > > > separable models; except for space x time, separable
> > > > > > > > > kronecker
> > > > > > > > > models are mostly avoided in geostatistical problems.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Finn
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > On Tue, 13 Oct 2020 at 04:17, Jonathan Judge
> > > > > > > > > <bach...@gmail.com>
> > > > > > > > > wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > The mgcv package makes it fairly easy to set up a
> > > > > > > > > > thin
> > > > > > > > > > plate
> > > > > > > > > > regression spline, even in multiple dimensions for
> > > > > > > > > > measurements on different scales (e.g., angles,
> > > > > > > > > > speed,
> > > > > > > > > > or
> > > > > > > > > > time).
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Consider the models: y ~ s(x1, x2) or even y ~ s(x1,
> > > > > > > > > > x2,
> > > > > > > > > > x3),
> > > > > > > > > > with the x variables being vectors of different
> > > > > > > > > > kinds of
> > > > > > > > > > numeric measurements . The default "tp" basis tends
> > > > > > > > > > to
> > > > > > > > > > work
> > > > > > > > > > quite well, but tensor / Kronecker options and
> > > > > > > > > > others
> > > > > > > > > > are of
> > > > > > > > > > course available also.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Is there an INLA equivalent for a multi-dimensional
> > > > > > > > > > smoother
> > > > > > > > > > for data like this that tends to work well with some
> > > > > > > > > > default
> > > > > > > > > > settings? If a mesh is required, are there
> > > > > > > > > > reasonably
> > > > > > > > > > robust
> > > > > > > > > > settings that can be specified relative to quantiles
> > > > > > > > > > or
> > > > > > > > > > some
> > > > > > > > > > other aspect of the x vectors?  Most mesh examples I
> > > > > > > > > > have seen
> > > > > > > > > > involve spatial coordinates only and even if they
> > > > > > > > > > apply
> > > > > > > > > > to my
> > > > > > > > > > situation I am struggling to see what good defaults
> > > > > > > > > > would be.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > For what it is worth, the one-dimensional spde
> > > > > > > > > > smoother
> > > > > > > > > > function provided by the BRINLA bri.adapt.prior
> > > > > > > > > > works
> > > > > > > > > > incredibly well and keeps much of the machinery
> > > > > > > > > > under
> > > > > > > > > > the
> > > > > > > > > > hood; perhaps there is a generalizable multi-
> > > > > > > > > > dimensional
> > > > > > > > > > version of it? I am also aware of the rw2 / rw2d
> > > > > > > > > > option,
> > > > > > > > > > but
> > > > > > > > > > it seems that may require a regularly-spaced lattice
> > > > > > > > > > and
> > > > > > > > > > I'm
> > > > > > > > > > not sure that is desirable for this application
> > > > > > > > > > (perhaps
> > > > > > > > > > it
> > > > > > > > > > is: others will know more than me).
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I have also tried Simon's ginla function, which may
> > > > > > > > > > also
> > > > > > > > > > offer
> > > > > > > > > > an avenue, but I am not quite sure if it is what I
> > > > > > > > > > am
> > > > > > > > > > looking
> > > > > > > > > > for either.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Would appreciate any suggestions.  Many thanks.

messages.subject: Right-truncated gamma
messages.subject_clean: Right-truncated gamma
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Is there a possibility to fit an INLA model that uses a right-truncated
gamma distribution, or to do something similar to that?

The case at hand is a hurdle gamma model for phreatic groundwater depth
in wetlands. The gamma part should probably be truncated since this
response, 'by nature', will never be larger than, say, 10 or 20 meter
(in the dataset, the maximum is below 3.5 meter anyway). The fitted
hurdle gamma model is sensible, except that when simulating numerous
data, occasional values even above 100 meter do occur, i.e. far outside
the realistic range.

Kind regards

Floris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Floris,

When the problem is only in the simulated values, you could simply truncate the simulated values. I don't expect to model parameters to be different when you truncate the distribution at a level outside the range of the data.

Maybe you could rescale the response to the [0, 1] interval and use a beta distribution with added point masses at 0 and 1.

Best regards,

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for these suggestions Thierry.

Tried truncation of simulated data, truncating at value 10. If I understand you right, you mean replacing values > 10 by value 10 (right-censoring); at least that's below approach—an alternative might be to replace them with new simulated values, i.e. discard extremes. In the log-scale, the artificial effect becomes a bit more apparent, but it seems still acceptable to me.

Rescaling to prepare for a beta distribution and adding an extra bernouilli submodel to include the value of 1 may be a good alternative, but indeed it may be unnecessary in this case.

Kind regards

Floris

messages.body_plain:
Thanks! I've never been into survival modelling, but will have a look
how this fits in.

Regarding the route of 'truncating simulated data', it's probably most
elegant to truncate the gamma density function first, and then simulate
from that. E.g.
https://www.r-bloggers.com/2020/08/generating-data-from-a-truncated-distribution/.
I think it's equivalent with dropping too extreme data and replacing
them with new values, but does it more directly.

Floris

messages.body_plain:
The source of the problem in the usecase is more complex it seems, than my initial thought about the width of the gamma distribution.

>From closer inspection of the extreme simulated observations (above value 10), it appears that two sources contribute to ± the same extent in generating extreme responses (which represent about 0.2% of the total simulated observations):
the linear predictor LPi of the gamma submodel (the gamma mean being exp(LPi)), so this is another obvious source. The extreme values at this level are all caused by extreme sampled values from either of three gaussian distributions, i.e. corresponding to three iid random effects
the gamma distribution itself, as discussed before

Maybe truncating the four involved distributions (3 x gaussian, 1 x gamma), when simulating, would be a fine solution, but first will have a look how inla.surv may help.

Floris

messages.body_plain:
you can try this one. 'constr=2' on generic2 will only sum-to-zero the
second half.

'generic2' is no longer needed as you can do your _0 and the 'trick' at
the end. this was not available at the time generic2 was added

On Thu, 2022-02-17 at 08:19 -0800, Thomas F Johnson wrote:
> Previous code example was incorrect. Here is a better example, with a
> residual, phylogeny, and species precision each set at 1.
>
>
> #Load packages
> library(INLA)
> library(mvtnorm)
> library(ape)
> species_n = 250 #100 species
> tr = rtree(species_n) #Generate a phylogeny for these species
> vcv = vcv.phylo(tr) #And produce a variance-covariance matrix
> prec_mat = solve(vcv) #Convert to a precision matrix
>
> prec_phy = 1 #And overall residual error
> prec_spec = 1 #And overall residual error
> prec_gau = 1 #And overall residual error
>
> trait = rmvnorm(1, mean = rep(prec_phy^-1,species_n), vcv) #Estimate a
> trait value for each species from a MVN()
> phytools::phylosig(tr, trait[1,], method = "lambda")
> trait2 = trait + rnorm(species_n, 0, sqrt(prec_spec^-1))
> phytools::phylosig(tr, trait2[1,], method = "lambda")
>
> #Next, prodcue a dataset describing the above trait value for 100
> individuals of each species
> indiv_n = 10 #With 100 individuals per species
> cmb_df = NULL
> for(a in c(1:species_n)){
>   df = data.frame(
>     species = a,
>     y = trait2[a] + rnorm(indiv_n, 0, sqrt(1 / prec_gau)) #Variance
> between individuals in a species
>   )
>   cmb_df = rbind(cmb_df, df)
> }
> #Add overall residual error
>
> ggplot(cmb_df[c(1:250),]) + #Plot of the first 10 species
>   geom_density(aes(x = y)) +
>   facet_wrap(species~.)
>
> #Run the following model
> pc_prior_gen0 = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param =
> c(sd(cmb_df$y)*3,0.1)))
> cmb_df$phylogeny = cmb_df$species
> m4_0 <- inla(y ~ 1 +
>                f(species, model = "iid", constr = T, hyper =
> pc_prior_gen0) +
>                f(phylogeny, model = "generic0", Cmatrix = prec_mat,
> constr = T, hyper = pc_prior_gen0),
>              data = cmb_df, family = "gaussian",
>              control.inla = list(force.diagonal = T))
> summary(m4_0)
>
> pc_prior_gen2 = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param =
> c(sd(cmb_df$y)*3,0.1)), prec.random = list(prior="pc.prec", param =
> c(sd(cmb_df$y)*3,0.1)))
> m4_2 = inla(y ~
>               f(phylogeny, model = "generic2", Cmatrix = prec_mat,
> constr = T, hyper = pc_prior_gen2),
>             data = cmb_df, family = "gaussian",
>             control.inla = list(force.diagonal = T))
> summary(m4_2)
>
> m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[1]^-1 #Residual variance model 0
> m4_2$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[1]^-1 #Residual variance model 2
>
> m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[3]^-1 #Variance captured by the
> phylogeny model 0
> m4_2$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[2]^-1# Variance captured by the
> phylogeny model 2
>
> m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[2]^-1 #Variance captured by the non-
> phylogenetic effect in model 0 e.g. individual variation
> (phylovar_2/m4_2$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[3]) - phylovar_2
> #Variance captured by the non-phylogenetic effect in model 2 e.g.
> individual variation
>
> m4_2$summary.fixed$sd/m4_0$summary.fixed$sd #SD around intercept is
> nearly 2x larger in the generic2 model
>
>
> On Thursday, 17 February 2022 at 11:15:30 UTC Thomas F Johnson wrote:
> > TLDR: My question - why I am getting such different estimates of the
> > phylogeny and species variances, as well as intercept SD under
> > generic0 and generic2?
> >
> > A common statistical approach to address non-independence in
> > phylogenetic comparative analyses is to use species' shared
> > evolutionary past to specify species covariances.
> >
> > From my understanding, INLAs generic0 and generic2 provide a
> > convenient approach to handle these species covariances using the
> > Cmatrix argument. Imagine a dataset where a trait (e.g. body mass)
> > has been estimated for 100 species, and this trait has high
> > phylogentic signal (traits are more similar in closely related
> > species). Within each species, body mass has been measured for 100
> > individuals, with a within species precision in body mass of 10. See
> > example below
> >
> > #Load packages
> > library(INLA)
> > library(mvtnorm)
> > library(ape)
> > library(ggplot2)
> > set.seed(1)
> > species_n = 100 #100 species
> > tr = rtree(species_n) #Generate a phylogeny for these species
> > vcv = vcv.phylo(tr) #And produce a variance-covariance matrix
> > P = solve(vcv) #Convert to a precision matrix
> > trait = rmvnorm(1, mean = rep(1,species_n), vcv) #Estimate a trait
> > value for each species from a MVN()
> >
> > #Next, prodcue a dataset describing the above trait value for 100
> > individuals of each species
> > indiv_n = 100 #With 100 individuals per species
> > prec_ind = 10 #With a given variance
> > prec_gau = 10 #And overall residual error
> > cmb_df = NULL
> > for(a in c(1:species_n)){
> >   df = data.frame(
> >     species = a,
> >     y = trait[a] + rnorm(indiv_n, 0, sqrt(1 / prec_ind)) #Variance
> > between individuals in a species
> >   )
> >   cmb_df = rbind(cmb_df, df)
> > }
> > cmb_df$y = cmb_df$y + rnorm(nrow(cmb_df), 0, sqrt(1 / prec_gau))
> > #Add overall residual error
> >
> > ggplot(cmb_df[c(1:1000),]) + #Plot of the first 10 species
> >   geom_density(aes(x = y)) +
> >   facet_wrap(species~.)
> >
> > Now, from this dataset, we want to extract the following parameters:
> > the intercept and its variance, as well as the variance captured by
> > the residuals, the phylogenetic covariance matrix, and the non-
> > phylogenetic species effect. To extract these, we could run a model
> > like this:
> >
> > trait ~ intercept + phylogeny + species + residuals
> > phylogeny ~ N(0, tau_phylogenyP) #P represent the precision matrix
> > of relatedness
> > species ~ N(0, tau_species)
> >
> > Assuming I am correct, I have fit the following model using generic
> > 0 below, with a pc prior:
> >
> > #Run the following model
> > pc_prior_gen0 = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param =
> > c(sd(cmb_df$y)*3,0.1)))
> > cmb_df$phylogeny = cmb_df$species
> > m4_0 <- inla(y ~ 1 +
> >                f(species, model = "iid", constr = T, hyper =
> > pc_prior_gen0) +
> >                f(phylogeny, model = "generic0", Cmatrix = P, constr
> > = T, hyper = pc_prior_gen0),
> >              data = cmb_df, family = "gaussian",
> >              control.inla = list(force.diagonal = T))
> > summary(m4_0)
> >
> > A similar model to above can be fit with generic2, except the
> > species term is dropped as it is included implicitly within the
> > phylogeny term, as species is estimated conditionally on the
> > phylogeny
> >
> > changing from:
> >
> > phylogeny ~ N(0, tau_phylogenyP) #P represent the precision matrix
> > of relatedness
> > species ~ N(0, tau_species)
> >
> > to:
> > phylogeny ~ N(0, tau_phylogenyP) #P represent the precision matrix
> > of relatedness
> > species ~ N(phylogeny, tau_species)
> >
> > And in INLA this model would look like:
> >
> > pc_prior_gen2 = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param =
> > c(sd(cmb_df$y)*3,0.1)), prec.random = list(prior="pc.prec", param =
> > c(sd(cmb_df$y)*3,0.1)))
> > m4_2 = inla(y ~
> >               f(phylogeny, model = "generic2", Cmatrix = P, constr =
> > T, hyper = pc_prior_gen2),
> >             data = cmb_df, family = "gaussian",
> >             control.inla = list(force.diagonal = T))
> > summary(m4_2)
> >
> > When you compare the outputs of generic0 and generic2, the residual
> > variance is the same, but the species and phylogeny variance always
> > differ. Further, whilst the intercept is the same, the intercepts
> > standard deviation is normally twice the size in generic2 relative
> > to generic0. See below:
> >
> > m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[1]^-1 #Residual variance model 0
> > m4_2$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[1]^-1 #Residual variance model 2
> >
> > m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[3]^-1 #Variance captured by the
> > phylogeny model 0
> > m4_2$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[2]^-1# Variance captured by the
> > phylogeny model 2
> >
> > m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[2]^-1 #Variance captured by the
> > non-phylogenetic effect in model 0 e.g. individual variation
> > (m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[2]^-
> > 1/m4_2$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[3]) -
> > m4_0$summary.hyperpar$`0.5quant`[2]^-1 #Variance captured by the
> > non-phylogenetic effect in model 2 e.g. individual variation
> >
> > m4_2$summary.fixed$sd/m4_0$summary.fixed$sd #SD around intercept is
> > nearly 2x larger in the generic2 model
> >
> > My question - why I am getting such different estimates of the
> > phylogeny and species variances, as well as intercept SD under
> > generic0 and generic2?
> >
> > Similar issues have discussed
> > here: https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/wRNZCqqT
> > RVQ/m/jzvR8ufSBAAJ
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Tom

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was running the preferential sampling model illustrated here: https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ch-lcox.html#sec:prefsampl

I also ran the inlabru version of the model on the same data (the data is exactly the same as in the example provided in the link). The results produced by inlabru is way off. Below is my code in plain INLA (copied from the link example):

win <- owin(c(0, 3), c(0, 3))
npix <- 300
spatstat.options(npixel = npix)
beta0 <- 3
exp(beta0) * diff(range(win$x)) * diff(range(win$y))
sigma2x <- 0.2
range <- 1.2

set.seed(1)
lg.s <- rLGCP('matern', beta0, var = sigma2x,
              scale = range / sqrt(8), nu = 1, win = win)

xy <- cbind(lg.s$x, lg.s$y)[, 2:1]

n <- nrow(xy)

Lam <- attr(lg.s, 'Lambda')
rf.s <- log(Lam$v)
summary(as.vector(rf.s))

loc.d <- 3 * cbind(c(0, 1, 1, 0, 0), c(0, 0, 1, 1, 0))
v_mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc.domain = loc.d, offset = c(0.3, 1),
                     max.edge = c(0.3, 0.7), cutoff = 0.05)
nv <- v_mesh$n

spv <- SpatialPoints(cbind(lg.s$x, lg.s$y))

dmesh <- inla.mesh.dual(v_mesh) # this function is the book.mesh.dual() function provided in the link for computing the dual mesh

plot(dmesh)

nv <- v_mesh$n

domain.polys <- Polygons(list(Polygon(loc.d)), '0')
domainSP <- SpatialPolygons(list(domain.polys))

plot(domainSP)

w <- sapply(1:length(dmesh), function(i) {
  if (gIntersects(dmesh[i, ], domainSP))
    return(gArea(gIntersection(dmesh[i, ], domainSP)))
  else return(0)

messages.body_plain:
Is there some kind of internal reparameterization in inlabru compared to plain INLA? Or some form of behind the scene operation that is different than plain INLA? It does not make sense that inlabru is supposed to be more accurate than plain INA but inlabru is now the one not giving the correct results. Thanks!

David

messages.body_plain:
What R version do you have? I switched from names(list(…)) to …names(), but perhaps should have checked if …names() was too new to use at this point? You can try installing from a specific commit; anything before yesterday won’t have …names() in it.

The lgcp accuracy is in the likelihood implementation, where inlabru uses a more accurate construction for the likelihood. Your inla code uses a different construction. It’s possible that the inlabru version is more sensitive to clustering, which increases the needed variance. But I’ll need to run the code here to check.

Finn
